transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says the administration is still working to figure
out what caused the technical glitch that brought the U.S. air travel system to a halt
on Friday, NPR's Joe Hernandez reports.
Officials say the problems began on Friday when the federal contractor L3Harris was installing
a new router at a site in El Dorado, Arkansas.
Secretary Duffy said on CNBC that the router is now at the contractor's lab in Florida
where analysts are working to figure out what went wrong.
I have the FAA staff on site.
I called Cash Patel and said, "Cash, would you send your agents just to make sure everything
per the FBI's thought process, it's all being done right?"
Duffy says there's no indication that Friday's disruption was caused by a cyber attack.
The nationwide groundstop lasted around four hours, but had ripple effects well beyond
that day.
It was only the second of its kind since the 9/11 terrorist attacks in 2001.
Joe Hernandez, NPR News.
United Airlines says it has resolved a technology problem that delayed departing flights today.
The Chicago-based airline said there was no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related
issue.
The Supreme Court has refused to hear a case about how the judiciary handles employee misconduct
cases and PRS Kerry Johnson reports justices denied a petition from a former public defender.
Karen Strickland says she suffered sexual harassment on the job in North Carolina.
She reported the abuse through the judiciary's internal system and went on to sue over the
issue, but the Supreme Court rejected her petition with no public dissent.
Strickland says her case exposed structural flaws in the judiciary's process for handling
workplace misconduct because the judiciary has refused to police itself, Strickland says.
The ball is now squarely in Congress' court to protect the 30,000 people who work for
the federal courts.
An NPR investigation found law clerks and other court workers hesitate to report problems
because they fear retaliation.
Kerry Johnson, NPR News.
A new survey of business executives suggests inflation may get worse before it gets better.
Republican PRS Scott Horsley reports on the latest findings from the Cleveland Federal
Reserve Bank.
CEOs surveyed by the bank say, on average, they expect to raise their prices by 3.7 percent
over the next year.
That's a bigger price hike than executives were projecting six months ago, but it's still
not big enough to cover the higher costs they expect their own companies to face.
CEOs project their costs will climb by more than 4 percent.
That's also up from the previous survey.
The Federal Reserve tries to limit inflation to just 2 percent per year, but prices have
been climbing faster than that for over five years now.
The central bank is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate next month in an effort
to tamp down demand and bring price hikes under control.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
NVIDIA led another sell-off in tech stocks today and helped drag the U.S. market lower.
This is NPR News.
Russia says it intercepted more than 1,300 Ukrainian drones in the latest barrage.
The massive attack was Kiev's largest since Russia's full-scale invasion nearly five years
ago.
Ukraine has increased its assaults on Russian oil refineries and supply routes.
Ukrainian President Zelensky claims these attacks have disabled over 55 percent of Russia's
oil refining capacity, though this remains unverified.
The Trump administration officially repealed a Biden-era rule meant to make federal child
care providers' salaries more competitive, and PR's Sequoia Corrillo reports.
The Trump administration published a final rule in the Federal Register on Monday to
roll back a Biden-era policy that would have raised educator salaries in the nation's largest
federal child care program, Head Start.
The rule was finalized in 2024 and would have gone into effect in 2031.
This move is part of a broader push by the administration to deregulate the program.
They estimate these changes will result in over $2 billion in cost savings.
But Head Start advocates argue that in order to maintain quality services and attract talent
to Head Start centers, the program needs to reevaluate how much it pays its workers.
Sequoia Corrillo, NPR News.
A Georgia O'Keefe painting dug out of a New York City closet after being stashed away
since the 1980s is expected to bring more than $3 million when it goes up for auction
this week.
Christie says the painting from 1930 was likely the first in a series of three.
It's an early example from a time when O'Keefe became enamored with the American Southwest.
The family of a woman who died earlier this year says she received the painting as a gift
in the 1960s.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says the FAA air travel shutdown was a technical glitch, not a cyberattack
United Airlines says it resolved a technology problem that delayed departing flights
Supreme Court declines to hear former North Carolina public defender Karen Strickland's judiciary harassment case
Cleveland Fed survey shows CEOs expect 3.7 percent price hikes, inflation may worsen
NVIDIA leads a tech stock sell-off that drags the U.S. market lower
